title: Finite separable subfield of a normal extension with finite automorphism group
statement: Let $k\subseteq E$ be an algebraic field extension [def-pc-field-extension]: every element of $E$ satisfies a nonzero polynomial over $k$. Assume it is normal, meaning that the minimal polynomial over $k$ of every element of $E$ splits into linear factors in $E[T]$, and that the group $\operatorname{Aut}_k(E)$ of field automorphisms fixing $k$ is finite. Let $E_s$ be the subfield of elements of $E$ separable over $k$ [def-weil-pbc-relative-separable-closure], where separable means that the minimal polynomial has no repeated roots. Then $E_s/k$ is finite-dimensional. No finite-dimensionality of $E/k$ is assumed.

source.place: Tag 0BME, lemma-lift-maps (2); Tag 0BR4, lemma-normal-embeddings-differ-by-aut; Tag 09HJ, lemma-separable-degree, applied only to finite separable subextensions; Tag 030K, lemma-separable-first. The finite-subextension degree bound is the field-theoretic inference used in pione.tex Tag 0BST, lemma-inertia-invariants-etale, second reduction paragraph.

proof.text: Put $G=\operatorname{Aut}_k(E)$ and $N=|G|\ge1$. The relative separable closure $E_s$ is a subfield containing $k$, and every element of $E_s$ is separable algebraic over $k$. For every finite list $a_1,\ldots,a_r\in E_s$, the field $k(a_1,\ldots,a_r)$ is finite over $k$ by the cited algebraic-generators theorem; it lies in $E_s$ because $E_s$ is a subfield, hence it is separable over $k$ by the elementwise definition. In particular the collection of finite intermediate fields $k\subseteq F\subseteq E_s$ is nonempty (it contains $k$).

source.place: Tag 030K, lemma-separable-first, and Tag 09GH, lemma-algebraic-finitely-generated; finite-subextension reduction

proof.text: Fix any finite intermediate field $k\subseteq F\subseteq E_s$ and put $d=[F:k]$. By the primitive-element theorem, $F=k(\alpha)$ for some $\alpha\in F$. Let $P\in k[T]$ be its monic minimal polynomial. It is separable since $\alpha\in E_s$. The power-basis theorem gives the basis $1,\alpha,\ldots,\alpha^{d-1}$ of $F/k$. To check explicitly that $\deg P=d$, express $\alpha^d$ in this basis: the resulting monic polynomial of degree $d$ annihilates $\alpha$, so minimality gives $\deg P\le d$. If $\deg P<d$, the relation $P(\alpha)=0$ contradicts the independence of this same basis. Thus $\deg P=d$.

source.place: Tag 030N, lemma-primitive-element (moreover clause); Tag 09GN, lemma-degree-minimal-polynomial, with the explicit basis argument

proof.text: Choose an algebraic closure $\Omega$ of $E$, and regard $k\subseteq E\subseteq\Omega$. The distinct-roots theorem applied to the monic separable polynomial $P$ over $k$ gives exactly $d$ roots in $\Omega$. Normality of $E/k$ says that $P$ already splits into linear factors over $E$. For a root $\beta\in\Omega$, evaluating that factorization gives a product of the factors $\beta-b$ with $b\in E$ equal to zero. Since $\Omega$ is a field, one factor vanishes, so $\beta\in E$. Thus $P$ has exactly $d$ distinct roots in $E$.

source.place: Tag 09GT, theorem-existence-algebraic-closure; normality and separability as in Tags 09HQ and 09HJ, lemma-separable-degree

proof.text: For every root $\beta\in E$ of $P$, the conjugacy theorem for algebraic normal extensions gives $\sigma\in G$ with $\sigma(\alpha)=\beta$. Conversely every $\sigma\in G$ sends $\alpha$ to a root of $P$, since it fixes its coefficients. Consequently $G\to\{\beta\in E:P(\beta)=0\}$, $\sigma\mapsto\sigma(\alpha)$, is surjective. Its finite target therefore has at most $N$ elements, proving $[F:k]=d\le N$ for every finite intermediate $F\subseteq E_s$. The cited conjugacy theorem requires algebraicity and normality of $E/k$, both hypotheses of the item, and does not require $F/k$ to be normal or $E/k$ finite.

source.place: Tag 0BME, lemma-lift-maps (2), specialized to roots of the primitive element; finite counting

proof.text: The set $D=\{[F:k]:k\subseteq F\subseteq E_s,\ [F:k]<\infty\}$ is a nonempty subset of $\{1,\ldots,N\}$, so it has a maximum. Choose a corresponding field $F_0$ and a finite $k$-basis $b_1,\ldots,b_m$ of $F_0$. For any $a\in E_s$, step 1 shows that $F_1=k(b_1,\ldots,b_m,a)\subseteq E_s$ is finite over $k$. It contains $F_0$: every element of $F_0$ is a $k$-linear combination of the $b_i$. The maximum defining $F_0$ gives $[F_1:k]\le m$. The same basis is linearly independent in $F_1$, so if any $x\in F_1$ were outside its span, adjoining $x$ would give $m+1$ independent vectors: in a relation with nonzero coefficient of $x$, solve for $x$ to get a contradiction, and if that coefficient is zero use independence of the $b_i$. This contradicts $\dim_k F_1\le m$. Hence $F_1=F_0$, and in particular $a\in F_0$.

source.place: Elementary bounded-degree maximum argument completing the finite-subextension reduction used in pione.tex Tag 0BST, lemma-inertia-invariants-etale, second reduction paragraph

proof.text: Step 5 applies to every $a\in E_s$, so $E_s\subseteq F_0$. Since $F_0\subseteq E_s$ by construction, $E_s=F_0$. The latter is finite-dimensional over $k$, which proves the assertion. The argument never bounds the purely inseparable extension $E/E_s$ or assumes that $E/k$ is finite.

source.place: Conclusion of the bounded-degree maximum argument

proof_origin.place: Explicit finite-subextension and maximal-degree argument using Tags 030K, 09GH, 030N, 09GN, 09GT and 0BME (2); supplies the field-theoretic finiteness inference needed in pione.tex Tag 0BST.

reviewed.note: mechanical checks by tools/merge_delivery.py; mathematics reviewed in full by NT-cc-N5-eb9a65089 (reviewer sub-agent of L); spot-checked: Read the item in full. The split is statement-preserving with no new nodes: six steps, eight proof_deps, all of them Mathlib-leaf nodes whose statements I opened. Step 1: E_s is a subfield, and finitely many of its elements generate a finite extension (generators node). Step 2: primitive element, using finiteness and separability of F ⊆ E_s; power basis; deg P = d proved explicitly because the power-basis node does not state it. Step 3: an algebraic closure Ω of E and the distinct-roots node give d distinct roots, and normality puts them in E (evaluating the factorization). Step 4: the normal-conjugacy node (algebraic and normal, no finiteness needed) maps G onto the roots, so [F:k] ≤ |G|. Steps 5–6: an elementary maximal-degree argument gives E_s = F_0. Small cases: the perfect closure of F_p(t) shows E/k need not be finite; Q(∛2) shows normality is needed.
